title: Speak Mandarin Campaign objectives and its links to Chinese dialect heritage
asked: Mr Cai Yinzhou asked what the Speak Mandarin Campaign's current policy objectives are, whether its application to locally screened dialect films will be reviewed given that streaming and social media platforms face no such restriction, and whether mandatory Mandarin dubbing of dialect films has a measurable effect. Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan asked whether the Ministry's assessment of the campaign covers its impact on the use and transmission of Chinese dialects, how dialect use is tracked, and whether the campaign's framing and approach will evolve so that promoting Mandarin no longer comes at the expense of dialects as heritage.
asked_by: Mr Cai Yinzhou and Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan
response: The Speak Mandarin Campaign, launched in 1979, promotes a common language across the Chinese community so that Chinese Singaporeans from different dialect backgrounds can communicate and access Chinese culture through Mandarin, and the Minister said these objectives remain valid today. The Promote Mandarin Council regularly reviews the campaign, which has evolved from promoting Mandarin as a common language to strengthening appreciation of Singapore Chinese cultural identity and making Mandarin learning fun, under the tagline "Speak Mandarin? Yes, I can". On dialects, he said their use continues to decline as English displaces mother tongues, and that dialect arts groups, heritage practitioners and clan association dialect classes are supported as part of Singapore's cultural heritage.

key_points.point: The campaign was launched in 1979 and its objectives remain valid today.
key_points.speaker: Mr David Neo
key_points.quote: The Speak Mandarin Campaign was launched in 1979.

key_points.point: The Promote Mandarin Council, made up of volunteer private and public individuals, regularly reviews the campaign's framing, approach and objectives.
key_points.speaker: Mr David Neo
key_points.quote: regularly reviews the campaign to keep its framing, approach and objectives relevant and meaningful in Singapore's multicultural context

key_points.point: The campaign has shifted from promoting Mandarin as a common language to strengthening appreciation of Singapore Chinese cultural identity and making Mandarin learning fun.
key_points.speaker: Mr David Neo
key_points.quote: the campaign has evolved from promoting Mandarin as a common language, to strengthening their appreciation for our Singapore Chinese cultural identity and making the learning of Mandarin fun and enjoyable

key_points.point: The current tagline encourages everyone to learn Mandarin even as English becomes more dominant in daily life.
key_points.speaker: Mr David Neo
key_points.quote: encourages everyone to learn Mandarin even as English becomes more dominant in daily life

key_points.point: MSF and MOE are setting aside more curriculum time to expose young Chinese students to Mandarin, and older students with aptitude and interest can develop into bicultural talents.
key_points.speaker: Mr David Neo
key_points.quote: the Ministry of Social and Family Development and the Ministry of Education are setting aside more curriculum time to expose young Chinese students to Mandarin

key_points.point: Dialect use in Singapore has continued to decline as English displaces mother tongues.
key_points.speaker: Mr David Neo
key_points.quote: the use of dialects in Singapore, has continued to decline

key_points.point: The National Arts Council supports arts groups practising traditional dialect cultures, such as the Siong Leng Musical Association for Nanyin and Nam Hwa Opera for Teochew opera.
key_points.speaker: Mr David Neo
key_points.quote: the National Arts Council supports arts groups that practises traditional forms of dialect cultures such as the Siong Leng Musical Association, which preserves Nanyin and Nam Hwa Opera, the Teochew opera group

key_points.point: The National Heritage Board recognises and supports practitioners and groups transmitting Chinese dialect culture.
key_points.speaker: Mr David Neo
key_points.quote: The National Heritage Board recognises and supports practitioners and groups that transmit Chinese dialect culture.

key_points.point: Clan associations including Singapore Hokkien Huay Kuan, Teochew Poit Ip Huay Kuan and Hainan Hwee Kuan run regular dialect classes.
key_points.speaker: Mr David Neo
key_points.quote: Clan associations, such as the Singapore Hokkien Huay Kuan or the Teochew Poit Ip Huay Kuan and Hainan Hwee Kuan also conduct regular dialect classes for interested Singaporeans.

key_points.point: The Government welcomes ideas to preserve dialect cultures while upholding the importance of Mandarin, and will take in feedback and work with the community on further steps.
key_points.speaker: Mr David Neo
key_points.quote: The Government welcomes ideas to preserve dialect cultures while upholding the importance of Mandarin.

key_points.point: The Minister sought permission for MDDI to answer Questions 6 to 12 on the use of dialects in films before supplementary questions.
key_points.speaker: Mr David Neo
key_points.quote: may I seek your permission to allow the Ministry of Digital Development and Information (MDDI) to provide the answers to Question Nos 6 to 12

Whether mandatory Mandarin dubbing of dialect films has any measurable effect on the campaign
Whether the Ministry's assessment of the campaign's effectiveness includes indicators of its impact on the use and transmission of Chinese dialects
How the Ministry tracks whether dialects remain in active use
